entries.clue: Departed at the last minute (4)

blocks.note: the departed are the dead; newspapers use the same adjective before a dead person's name
arriving at the last minute is only just not behind time

annotation.surface: Someone left in a hurry, only just in time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Departed' reads as a verb, left; it is the adjective for the dead, as in 'the late king'.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: one sense is a polite word for dead, the other means happening at the end of the time allowed.

entries.clue: Clear ‘Hello!’ misread in French city (2,8)

indicatorNotes.misread: a misread word comes out with its letters in the wrong order

annotation.surface: A plainly written greeting gets misunderstood somewhere in France.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clear' looks like an adjective describing the greeting, but its letters are half the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a port city on the Atlantic coast of western France.

entries.clue: Government economist in battered trenchcoat (10)

indicatorNotes.battered: something battered is knocked out of shape

annotation.surface: A scruffy economist in a worn-out raincoat, like a TV detective.
annotation.walkthrough: TRENCHCOAT and TECHNOCRAT share every letter, which makes this one of the neatest anagram pairs in English.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a technical expert, such as an economist, put in charge of government.

entries.clue: Clairvoyancy of the Dark Ages? (10)

blocks.note: knowing the future before it happens: the reading the surface pushes
an era before scientific knowledge, read as a prefix plus a noun

annotation.surface: A question about fortune-tellers in medieval times.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer as PRE-SCIENCE and it describes an age before science; read as one word it means foreknowledge.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean knowing things before they happen.

entries.clue: Tells one that might be Des: About 1? (7)

blocks.note: surface padding hinting at the entertainer Des O'Connor, who died in 2020

annotation.surface: A cryptic remark about someone called Des.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One that might be Des' is a late person: the entertainer Des O'Connor died in 2020, so he is 'the late Des'. RE plus a plural of LATE makes RELATES.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to relate a story is to tell it.

entries.clue: Weapon’s deployed, obtaining vegetable (4,3)

indicatorNotes.deployed: troops deployed are spread out and rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters; the apostrophe is ignored

annotation.surface: A weapon is used, and somehow a vegetable turns up.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Weapon’s' is surface dressing; take the letters WEAPONS.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a mangetout, a flat pea eaten pod and all.

entries.clue: Distribute dodgy enterprises (11)

indicatorNotes.dodgy: dodgy means unsound, not in proper shape

annotation.surface: An instruction to hand out shares in shady businesses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dodgy enterprises' reads as shady firms; 'dodgy' only says the letters are unreliable in their order.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean scattering things about among others.

entries.clue: Rear of capuchin monkey? Scruff of the neck (4)

indicatorNotes.Rear of: the rear of a word is its last letter

annotation.surface: A capuchin monkey's backside, then someone grabbed by the collar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capuchin monkey' reads as one animal; only the capuchin's tail letter is used, and 'monkey' alone gives APE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name the back of the neck, where a mother cat grips her kitten.

entries.clue: Otherwise, university in London’s backing English (4)

indicatorNotes.backing: to back something is to stand behind it in support, so LSE goes after E

blocks.note: the London School of Economics, part of the University of London

annotation.surface: A London university supports English studies, or perhaps not.
annotation.walkthrough: The LSE is the London School of Economics; 'backing' puts it behind E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in 'hurry, or else'.

entries.clue: Successfully wear dress that’s not loud (4)

indicatorNotes.that’s not: the dress is without the letter for loud

blocks.note: f = forte, loud in music; removed

annotation.surface: Advice to carry off a quiet, understated outfit.
annotation.walkthrough: F for loud comes from music notation (forte). 'Dress' looks like the thing worn, but it supplies FROCK.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to rock an outfit is to wear it with style and get away with it.

entries.clue: Infernal class of exercises taking time? Son, they could be positive (5,5)

indicatorNotes.taking: taking in the sense of taking on board: BLOODY absorbs the T inside it

blocks.note: PE = physical education, a school lesson

annotation.surface: A pupil grumbling about a hellish PE lesson that drags on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Positive' looks like an attitude but refers to rhesus factor: A-positive, O-positive and so on.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: groups such as O or AB come as positive or negative.

entries.clue: Puts in a call to Dover? Or Rugby? (7,5)

blocks.note: to get in touch with someone by phone
Dover is an English ferry port, an example of one

annotation.surface: Someone phoning Dover, or perhaps Rugby, two English towns.
annotation.walkthrough: Dover and Rugby are both English towns, so the surface reads as a list of places; Rugby is really the game.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: rugby involves tackling and scrums, so it is one such game.

entries.clue: Got arrested (11)

blocks.note: to get a point is to understand it
what police do to a suspect

annotation.surface: Someone was taken in by the police.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, 'got arrested'; split it into two separate meanings.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: the word means both understood and seized by police.

entries.clue: Stinking drunk, old and amorous (10)

indicatorNotes.drunk: a drunk person is all over the place

annotation.surface: An unflattering portrait of a smelly, tipsy, ageing Romeo.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stinking drunk' reads as one phrase, very drunk; 'Stinking' is the definition and 'drunk' stirs the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean foul-smelling.

entries.clue: Struggle in unpicking ancestries (10)

annotation.surface: A genealogist's struggle to untangle family trees.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unpicking ancestries' paints tracing a family tree, but it is an instruction to take the letters apart.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: fighting back against a force, as the wartime French underground did, is a struggle.

entries.clue: Ditches storage’s cap; escalates, in part (7)

indicatorNotes.in part: the answer is part of the words before it

blocks.note: the letters start at the end of storage's and run through the semicolon

annotation.surface: A note about removing a storage cap, then things escalating.
annotation.walkthrough: The punctuation breaks the surface into pieces, but the letters run straight across the apostrophe and semicolon.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: to ditch someone is to get away from them.

entries.clue: Pacify with a k-kind of pudding (7)

blocks.note: pease pudding, said with a stutter

annotation.surface: Calming someone down with a helping of pudding.
annotation.walkthrough: The stutter in 'k-kind' is the signal: the pudding word gets its first letter doubled too. Pease pudding is a British dish of boiled split peas.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean calming someone by giving in to them.

entries.clue: Encourages rising, sets off to go around North (7)

indicatorNotes.to go around: LEAVES goes around N, enclosing it

annotation.surface: Someone stirs up a revolt, then heads off on a trip up North.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Encourages rising' sounds like incitement to revolt; it is yeast making bread rise.
annotation.definitionFit: A baking sense: adding yeast or another raising agent makes dough rise.

entries.clue: Some wholesaler, nouveau-riche, somewhere on the Med (7)

indicatorNotes.Some: some of the letters that follow

blocks.note: starts at the sixth letter of wholesaler and ends two letters into nouveau

annotation.surface: A newly rich trader buys a place on the Mediterranean.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nouveau-riche' looks like a description of the wholesaler; it is only there to carry the last letters across the comma.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a port city in southern Italy, on the Mediterranean.

entries.clue: In Oxford at the outset, intensively study flipping electrical engineer (7)

indicatorNotes.at the outset: the outset of Oxford is its first letter
indicatorNotes.flipping: flipping turns the whole string back to front

blocks.note: to cram is to study hard before an exam

annotation.surface: A student flat out revising at Oxford.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a preposition placing the student in Oxford, but it is a piece of the answer. INOCRAM read backwards is MARCONI.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Guglielmo Marconi pioneered radio transmission.

entries.clue: Revered Hindu’s headgear pinched by parent (7)

indicatorNotes.pinched by: the hat is gripped between parts of the parent

blocks.note: a hat is headgear; goes inside MAMA

annotation.surface: A holy man's hat is stolen by someone's mother.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pinched' looks like stolen; it means squeezed in between.
annotation.definitionFit: A title of respect: it is an honorific for a revered Hindu sage, as with Gandhi.

entries.clue: Hotel’s rather fancy – here? (6,6)

annotation.surface: A remark that a hotel is rather posh, asking where you are.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a spa is exactly where you'd find a rather fancy hotel.
annotation.definitionFit: An &lit: read straight, the clue describes an upmarket spa where the hotels are rather fancy.

entries.clue: Go round with would-be fiancé’s offering (4)

blocks.note: to encircle, as a fence does a field
what a suitor traditionally holds out when proposing

annotation.surface: A suitor calls round with a gift for his intended.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go round' suggests visiting; it means encircling.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: a verb for encircling and the band given at an engagement.

entries.clue: Crossword setter’s written up mother’s novel (4)

indicatorNotes.written up: in a down clue, writing up turns a word bottom to top

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as ME

annotation.surface: The setter has written a book about their mother.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Setter’s written up' reads as having written something; the ’s is 'has', and 'up' turns ME over.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Jane Austen's 1815 novel about a meddling matchmaker.

entries.clue: Everyman’s … average. ‘Rank’? That’s too much (10)

blocks.note: Everyman is the setter, so 'Everyman is' = I'M
surface padding: the setter quoting an insult to shrug it off

annotation.surface: The setter shrugs off being called 'rank': only average, and that insult goes too far.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for 'I', so Everyman’s = I'M. 'Rank' belongs to the surface joke, though rank can itself mean excessive.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean going beyond reasonable limits.

entries.clue: When nothing changes if you turn back time? (4)

annotation.definition: When nothing changes if you turn back time?

blocks.note: a moment when all is static: the reading the surface pushes
reads as putting the clocks back; really, reading a time word right to left

annotation.surface: A musing on clocks going back an hour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turn back time' sounds like the clocks changing; it means writing the time word backwards, and NOON is a palindrome.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: a time of day that reads the same both ways.

entries.clue: Sum like ‘125 x 8’? (5,5)

blocks.note: the product is a thousand, and slang for a thousand is a word that also means great

annotation.surface: A maths question about multiplication.
annotation.walkthrough: 125 times 8 makes 1,000, and a grand is slang for a thousand pounds or dollars.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the final figure at the foot of a bill is the sum of all its lines.

entries.clue: Man, perhaps, in audition the writer’s going to (4)

indicatorNotes.in audition: an audition is a hearing, so the words are to be heard

blocks.note: the writer = I; 'I'll' = I will, I'm going to

annotation.surface: An actor hoping to land the part in an audition.
annotation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea; 'Man' looks like a person here.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Man is a small island in the Irish Sea, a Crown dependency.
